newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST - Australian Business News - Aug 20.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Australian Business News - Aug 20.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Following criticism from institutional investors, BHP chief executive John Prescott said yesterday the Big Australian has set itself a May 1998 deadline for selling or restructuring any underperforming assets. Prescott added that the company would reduce its debt by a further A$1.5 billion within the same period. Page 1.

Under a A$6 million rescue deal announced yesterday, father and son racing identities Bill and Robbie Waterhouse will subscribe for 70 million shares in troubled video distributor Network Entertainment Ltd at one cent each, giving them a stake of over 75 pe cent and releasing Network from its bank debt. Page 17.

Despite reporting one of its strongest trading profits since 1989, John Fairfax Holdings Ltd said abnormal writedowns from redundancies and restructuring costs, along with a A$27 million increase in depreciation charges on the new Chullora plant, worked towards a 15.4 per cent drop in full-year net profit to A$74 million. Page 17.

Australian Provincial Newspapers Holdings Ltd chief executive Cameron O'Reilly said that while the company has reported a 25 per cent increase in net profit to A$14.39 million for the six months to June, it faces a A$30 million claim against it from the Australian Taxation Office. Page 18.

While Foxtel shareholders Telstra and News Corp agreed to take the merger deal with Australis Media Ltd to conclusion, the deal, which is planned to go ahead a month before the A$12 billion public float of Telstra, is yet to get approval from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. Page 18.

Following concerns about its A$150 million capital raising, and reports that more independent supermarkets have defected to Woolworths' Australian Independent Wholesalers, Davids Ltd's share price yesterday slumped to a record low of 78 cents, despite a sight increase in the All Ordinaries. Page 19.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Shares in John Fairfax fell 7 cents yesterday immediately after the company reported a 15 per cent drop in profit to A$74 million. The publisher said the result reflected poor advertising sales that followed on from a continued depressed economy, yet said it is pleased with the result given the current economic conditions. Page 23.

The new Retail Meter '97 survey, compiled by Coopers & Lybrand and the Australian Centre for Retail Studies at Monash University, has found that despite tough trading conditions, individual retailers are overly optimistic, with the majority expecting to outperform the general retail market in the next year. Page 23.

Following negative investor sentiment, costs blowouts and the departure of three senior executives, BHP managing director John Prescott said yesterday it will no longer be "business as usual" at BHP, with up to three outside directors to be appointed to the board, and a reduced capital commitment expected for the steel division. Page 23.

In what could be another impediment to State revenue, Ansett Australia is planning to challenge the States' right to impose payroll taxes on its airport-based employees. Success for Ansett could set a precedent for other employers who operate on Commonwelth-owned or controlled property, and could result in millions of dollars worth of retrospective tax refunds. Page 25.

Peter Lehmann Wines yesterday recorded a record 43 per cent increase in after-tax profits to A$2.6 million, just four years after its sharemarket listing. The results follow an increase in sales of 29 per cent to A$22.1 million for the 12 months to June 30, and reflect improved export market sales for the year. Page 25.

CSL managing director Brian McNamee said yesterday the company recorded a 21 per cent rise in annual net profit to A$35.1 million thanks to strong demand for its vaccines, the continued focus on branded product sales, increased bioplasma plant throughput and a general tightening of costs. Page 25.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

In an address to the Securities Institute of Australia, BHP chief executive John Prescott sought to reassure the investment community with a pledge that the company will demolish its boardroom power with the appointment of three independent directors. Prescott added that the days of viewing BHP as the Big Australian were over. Page 29.

Australian Football League chief executive Wayne Jackson announced yesterday the AFL Commission has decided not to link television rights with the Docklands stadium project in Melbourne. Jackson said the AFL's position on the issue would be clearer by the end of next week. Page 29.

The Reserve Bank's Quarterly Economic Report in its August Bulletin says infrastructure projects in Sydney and Melbourne, mainly in the housing and business construction sectors, can boost economic growth, and in turn, reduce Australia's high unemployment rate. Page 29.

Network Entertainment co-founder and chief executive Karl O'Farrell, a 33 per cent stakeholder in the video distribution group, said yesterday he is excited about the rescue deal that will see Robbie and Bill Waterhouse buying a 77.7 per cent holding in the company that will take the group out of voluntary administration and give the Waterhouses control. Page 29.

In the Labor Party's first response to the Wallis report into Australia's financial systems, Federal shadow Treasurer Gareth Evans said yesterday the Federal Opposition strongly approves of the report's recommendations for an overhaul of prudential regulation, but is less sure on the consumer protection reforms, and strongly rejects the report's "open slather" on bank fees. Page 31.

The Brisbane District Court heard yesterday that Phillip Henry Winkless and Arthur John Forrest, the former directors of Australian Coachlines Holdings, sold shares in the company using information that was not known to the public. The two face charges of insider trading for events that took place in March 1993. Page 31.
THE AGE

While announcing a 21 per cent lift in after-tax net profit to A$35.1 million for pharmaceutical group CSL, its managing director Brian McNamee said the Federal Government's latest industry policies recognised what was required to attract investment to a small economy, and reacted to long-held concerns expressed by Australia's industry leaders. Page B1.

During a landmark address to the Securities Institute of Australia in Sydney, BHP chief executive John Prescott announced a boardroom restructure that follows institutional demands that the company be more dynamic. Under the restructure, three independent directors will be added to the board. Page B1.

Network Entertainment's chief creditor, the Commonwealth Bank, has accepted a rescue deal for Network that will see Robbie Waterhouse and his father Bill Waterhouse take control of the video distribution group and pull it out of voluntary administration. The Waterhouses will be given A$700,000 worth of shares to take 77.7 per cent of Network. Page B1.

Freight giant TNT and fellow industry companies Streetline, Mayne Nickless and Federal Express have suggested in a proposal to the National Competition Council that parts of Australia Post's supply chain should be tendered out, and the Federal Government hould look at whether a uniform 45 cents nationwide standard mail service is fair. Page B3.

Toyota Manufacturing Company president Hiroshi Okuda said yesterday at the Gold Coast launch of the new Camry/Vienta range that no decision has yet been made over the future of Corolla production at Toyota's Altona car plant. The comments followed suggestions that the production of the new Avalon would take over from the Corolla. Page B3.

Australian Securities Commission chairman Alan Cameron said yesterday the ASC would investigate sections of the Corporations Law if the Corporations and Securities panel approves key share trades in John Fairfax Holdings Ltd between broking house Merrill Lynch and New Zealand-based Brierley Investments Ltd. Page B3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
